**Unit question:** How should a materials engineer judge a computational result?

::: {.callout-warning}
## Prototype status

L01–L04 currently establish the textual and mathematical spine. They are not complete lecture packages. Figures, image permissions and alt text, Wooclap links, and executable notebooks remain in the [visual and interactive backlog](media-backlog.qmd). Sources are collected in the [Unit 0 references and source notes](references.qmd).
:::

The first four lectures use one recurring problem, estimating $\pi$, to separate four ideas that are often mixed together: the quality of a model, the convergence of a numerical method, the limitations of floating-point arithmetic, and the speed of an implementation.

1. [L01 · A numerical mindset for materials engineers](L01/index.qmd)
2. [L02 · Choosing and judging a numerical method](L02/index.qmd)
3. [L03 · Numbers inside a computer](L03/index.qmd)
4. [L04 · Making a computation faster](L04/index.qmd)

[Unit 0 references and source notes](references.qmd)

By the end of the unit, you should be able to explain why a result can be plausible but untrustworthy, compare methods using error and cost, recognize common finite-precision problems, and identify several ways to accelerate a calculation without assuming that faster is always better.
